summary: This informational memo documents MAPOS, a multiple access protocol that carries network datagrams, wrapped in HDLC frames, over SONET/SDH links.

plainLanguage.summary: MAPOS carries network datagrams in HDLC frames across SONET/SDH links. Frame switches use each frame's destination address so multiple nodes can share a switched network.

questions: what is the mapos frame format
subtitle: A link-layer protocol for carrying HDLC frames over shared SONET/SDH switch networks.

tldr.problem: SONET/SDH links are point-to-point, so using them to connect several nodes requires a way to provide multiple access and forward traffic between nodes.
tldr.mechanism: MAPOS carries datagrams in HDLC-like frames with destination addresses. Frame switches forward frames across a single switch or a cluster.
tldr.outcome: The Informational memo describes a connectionless link-layer protocol with broadcast and multicast support. It is not an IETF standards-track document.

today: RFC 2171 is an Informational memo and is not an IETF standards-track document. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What MAPOS Does
sections.content:
Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH (MAPOS) transmits network-protocol datagrams inside HDLC frames over SONET/SDH. Because SONET/SDH is inherently point-to-point, MAPOS uses frame switches to provide multiple access for LAN and WAN configurations.

A node places the destination address in a frame and sends it over the link. A switch forwards the frame using that address; clusters can forward it through multiple switches. MAPOS is connectionless and can carry network-layer protocols such as IP.
sections.plainLanguage: MAPOS adds destination-based frame forwarding to SONET/SDH links. A node sends a frame, and switches forward it toward the addressed node.

sections.title: Switches and Node Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC describes point-to-point links, a star arrangement with nodes connected to one frame switch, and clusters made from linked frame switches. Each switch port has an identifier unique within that switch, and a node connected to the port uses that address.

In a switch cluster, the address is divided into a switch part and a node-within-switch part using a subnet mask. An address may be configured manually or assigned using the mechanism described in RFC 2173.
sections.plainLanguage: A node's address comes from the switch port it uses. In a cluster, the address also identifies the switch.

sections.title: The MAPOS Frame
sections.content:
A frame contains a Flag, Address, Control, Protocol, Information field, Frame Check Sequence (FCS) and closing Flag. The flag sequence is 01111110 (0x7E); the 8-bit address carries the destination; and the control field is always 00000011 (0x03).

The 16-bit Protocol field identifies the encapsulated datagram. The Information field can be up to 65,280 octets. The FCS is 16 bits by default, with an optional 32-bit form. Address 0xFF is broadcast; the top address bit distinguishes unicast from multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: The frame marks its start and end, names its destination, identifies the carried protocol and includes an error-check value. The address can identify a single node, a multicast group or all nodes.

sections.title: Escaping Special Bytes
sections.content:
MAPOS uses octet stuffing because it treats SONET/SDH as a byte-oriented link. After calculating the FCS, the sender replaces any flag byte inside a frame with an escape sequence and also escapes the escape byte itself.

The receiver reverses those substitutions before computing the FCS. The sender separates frames with one or more flag sequences and sends flags during idle periods.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender changes flag bytes found inside a frame so they cannot be mistaken for frame boundaries. The receiver restores those bytes before checking the frame.

sections.title: SONET and SDH Interoperability
sections.content:
MAPOS treats the end-to-end SONET/SDH path as a transparent channel that delivers HDLC frames unaltered. Nodes and switches should terminate SONET/SDH overhead according to the relevant specifications, but SONET and SDH interpret some overhead differently.

The RFC points to differences in pointer bytes and in bytes that some implementations use for proprietary purposes. It encourages implementers to account for those differences and provide workarounds. The memo does not discuss security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: SONET and SDH can interpret some link overhead differently. Implementations need to account for those differences to exchange frames correctly.
